newsitem.title: USA: Ruling due next week in Tampa, Fla., bond lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Ruling due next week in Tampa, Fla., bond lawsuit.

text.p: A ruling is expected by Tuesday in a Florida lawsuit challenging the use of tax-backed bonds to build the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' new stadium, an assistant to Circuit Judge Sam Pendino said Thursday.

Five days of testimony ended late Wednesday in the legal dispute over the plan to issue $204.5 million of Tampa Sports Authority revenue bonds for the project. Smith Barney Inc is senior manager for the long-delayed deal.

The plaintiff, former Tampa Mayer Bill Poe, testified that the 65,000-steat stadium would unconstitutionally use public money for a project that would mainly benefit the privately owned football team. He said the city already has a stadium for the Bucs and does not need a new one.
"Hundreds of millions of dollars would be spent -- taxpayers' dollars -- for a second stadium," Poe said. "And that money would be for the benefit of private entities."

In September, voters approved a half-cent local-option sales tax to raise money for schools, public safety and the stadium. Construction began shortly after the referendum but the bond issue has been delayed by the lawsuit.
Poe's lawsuit against the City of Tampa and Hillsborough County was folded into a bond validation hearing sought by the county. The loser is expected to appeal directly to the Florida Supreme Court.
County Attorney Emeline Acton said Florida courts have validated bonds for stadiums and arenas in 31 other cases.

Mayor Dick Greco testified that it was in the public interest to build entertainment venues such as stadiums and performing arts centers because without them, "You'd have a city in a vacuum, with nothing but businesses."
Jack Wilson, former chairman of the Greater Tampa Chamber of Commerce, said Tampa gets valuable national publicity from the Bucs, who threatened to leave if they did not get a new stadium.

Sports economist Edward Shils, an instuctor a the Wharton School of Business in Philadelphia, estimated the team's annual economic impact on the Tampa area at $183 million. His estimate was based on a multiplyer effect, assuming each dollar brought in by the team has an impact of $2.60 in the community.

Ecnomists for the plaintiff disputed the figures. Poe's attorney, Chris Bently, said the public could end up paying at least $24 million in maintencance costs over the 30-year term of the lease because the reserve fund for maintenance will be exhausted long before the lease expires.
The contract calls for the Bucs to pay $3.5 million in annual rent for 30 years. It gives the team the first $2 million of profits from other stadium events, minus ticket sales.
